info.title: SiyahTuş API
info.description: The SiyahTuş HTTP API: chats, customers, tickets, webhooks and uploads. Generated from the contract the server itself is built against. Last changed 2026-11-07.

servers.description: Production (eu region; the us deployment serves us workspaces)

get.description:
Reports the process plus each backing store. Returns 200 only when every
dependency is reachable, so it is safe to use as a readiness probe.

The body has two shapes. An anonymous
caller — or one whose credential does not resolve to at least the
`admin` role — gets only `status` + `service`: version, region,
dependency latencies, scheduler and event-partition status and which
mock each provider runs are infrastructure detail an unauthenticated
caller has no business reading. An admin-role bearer token gets every
field below.
Either way the status code (200/503) reflects real dependency health —
narrowing applies to the body only, so an orchestrator that reads only
the status code is unaffected.

503.description: At least one dependency is unreachable

get.description:
Answers as soon as the process is accepting connections — no dependency
is touched, ever. This is what an orchestrator's LIVENESS probe should
point at: killing this process because Postgres is unreachable removes
the one thing that could still serve `/health/ready` again once the
dependency recovers, and the replacement process starts no better off.

200.description: The process is up. Always 200 — a down dependency does not affect this response.

get.description:
Probes Postgres and Redis for real and returns 503 when either is
unreachable, so an orchestrator takes the instance out of rotation. This
is the same dependency probe `/health` runs, but always answers the
narrow `{status, service}` body — an orchestrator probe never carries a
bearer token, so the admin-only detail `/health` can return would never
be reachable here anyway.

503.description:
Not ready. `status` says which kind: `degraded` — at least one
dependency is unreachable; `draining` — the process received SIGTERM
and is shutting down. Readiness turns false before the
server stops accepting, precisely so an orchestrator has a probe
interval in which to stop routing here while requests are still being
answered normally.

200.description: Caller identity, tenant and effective scopes

public_name.description:
Agent principals only. The name visitors see in the widget
instead of `name`; `null` means `name` is shown.

organization_name.description:
Agent principals only. The workspace's display name — shipped
with the profile the app already fetches on load, rather than a
second request, for a caller that has nowhere else to read it
(the mobile Settings → Account card, 13.7-r; the console reads
it from `/auth/login`'s membership list instead, which a
long-lived session never revisits).

region.description:
Where the caller's **workspace** keeps its data — the region
it named at signup and can never leave. Since a
deployment refuses anything else with 421, this is also
always the region answering the request.

scopes.description:
What this credential may do on this request. For an agent it
is resolved against the role the caller holds now and the
workspace's permission matrix: a sign-in
session follows the matrix both ways; a partner app's grant
and a personal access token keep their own list, less what
the matrix takes from the role.

capabilities.description:
Agent principals only. What the caller's role holds in this
workspace's permission matrix, every capability by
key — the panel's "Yetkilerim", and what a capability with no
scope of its own is read from. Resolved from the same matrix
snapshot as `scopes`.

onboarding_completed.description:
Agent principals only. Whether the workspace has finished (or
skipped) first-run setup — the shell gates the onboarding
wizard on this without a second request.

license.description:
Agent principals only, **every role**. What the
workspace may do right now — the same `access` that
`GET /billing/subscription` reports, but readable without a
billing scope, so the shell can tell an agent that the trial
is running out or over. Read once with the
profile, so a trial that ends mid-session is learned from
the `402 license_expired` the next write gets.

group_ids.description:
Agent principals only. The teams the caller belongs to: the console decides "a chat was handed to my team"
from a push that names only the receiving team's id. Read
with the profile; a change of membership shows from the next
read.

notification_preferences.description:
Agent principals only. Every channel the caller can be reached
through — per user, per license. Shipped
with the profile because the console's alerting decision runs
on every incoming message and cannot afford a fetch;
`/agents/me/notification-preferences` is the same object on
its own.

appearance.description:
Agent principals only. The panel font to paint — the later of
the workspace default and the caller's own choice — resolved
here so the panel never reapplies the rule itself.

two_factor.description:
Agent principals only. The caller's own second factor. Carried here rather than on an
endpoint of its own: it is a property of the caller, which is
what this route describes, and the account settings screen
has nowhere else to read "it is on, and three recovery codes
are left". Never carries the secret or any code.

enabled.description: An enrollment exists and has been confirmed with a code.

pending.description:
A secret has been issued but no code has confirmed it
yet — `POST /auth/2fa/enroll` was called and
`POST /auth/2fa/activate` was not.

recovery_codes_remaining.description: Unused codes left. Which ones is never retrievable.

impersonation.description:
Agent principals only, and only when a SiyahTuş operator is
signed in as this member from the root panel.
The console paints its red banner from it. Absent otherwise.

get.summary: List the caller's personal access tokens

200.description: Tokens (metadata only — the secret is never retrievable)

post.description:
The plaintext token is in this response and nowhere else — only its hash
is stored. A token cannot be granted scopes the creating session does not
already hold (403, `error.details.reason: scopes_not_held`, `scopes` the
comma-separated ones it lacks); a request left with no valid scope is a 400
with `reason: scopes_required`. Nor scopes the workspace's
permission matrix lends the caller's role beyond its default set — a token
keeps its list, and would outlive the loan (403, `reason:
scopes_not_delegable`, `scopes`; RL-02 · tm 325.3). Without `scopes`, the
token takes the role's default set as far as the session holds it.

get.description:
Returns chats the caller may see. An agent sees a chat only through a team
they belong to unless their token carries `chats--all:ro`. A member whose
role the workspace's permission matrix sets to `own` for `chats.view`
sees only the chats they are assigned to or have joined, whatever their
token carries; at `none` the request is a 403.

Paginated by opaque keyset cursor rather than offset: an offset page shifts
under you every time a new message arrives, which in an active inbox means
silently skipped conversations.

**Text search.** With `query` the list is a search of message
text: the conversations the caller may see — open and archived — that
hold a message containing every word of the query, newest match first,
each item carrying `match` (its newest matching message, cut to a
snippet). Case and Turkish letters are folded ("İSTANBUL" finds
"istanbul", "cagri" finds "çağrı"), words match anywhere and in any order
("papara 5000" finds "Papara ile 5000 TL"), `%` and `_` mean
themselves, and there is no stemming. Visitor and agent messages, AI
replies and internal notes are searched; system lines are not. A card
number was masked when it was written, so its digits find nothing.

A search reads messages from `date_from` (default: 90 days before
`date_to`) up to but not including `date_to` (default: now), at most
400 days. It composes with `date_from`, `date_to`, `limit` (default
50) and `page_id` only — any other filter, or `sort=oldest`, is a 400 —
and `total` is the number of matching conversations across all pages.
A query needs three letters or digits in a row in one of its words, at
most eight words and 1000 bytes; one that matches more than 20 000
messages is refused as too broad (400, `details.reason: too_broad`) —
add a word or narrow the dates. A search that runs out of time is a 503.
The request log masks `query`; it is never put in a browser address.

parameters.name: view
parameters.description:
`my` — assigned to the caller · `queued` — waiting for an agent ·
`unassigned` — routed but unclaimed · `supervised` — open and being
watched by the caller (a `chat_supervisions` row of theirs), which is
not the same question the Traffic board's `supervised` state asks —
that one is "is anybody watching this visitor right now" and is
bounded by the heartbeat window · `archived` — closed ·
`ai` — the AI agent is handling it (a bot has replied and no human
has), kept out of the human queue · `ai_solved` — closed with no
human reply and not handed off by the AI or a rule bot, i.e. an AI
resolution (ADR-09a, the same line billing counts) · `team` — open
and routed to a team the caller leads (`group_agents.is_lead`,
RL-03), whoever holds it, the AI included; empty for someone who
leads no team · `all` — every chat the caller may see.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description:
Narrows to the conversations that arrived over one messaging channel
— the inbox's channel views. An axis of its own, at
right angles to `view`: `view=my&channel=whatsapp` is the caller's
own WhatsApp conversations, and `total` counts the same intersection
the rows come from.

A chat's channel is the `channel_type` of its *oldest inbound*
`channel_messages` row — the definition Reports' channel split
already uses, so the rail and the report can never
disagree about which channel a conversation belongs to. Only adapter
channels can answer it: a conversation that arrived through the
website widget, a chat page or e-mail crossed no adapter and so
belongs to none of these values.

parameters.name: queue_group_id
parameters.description:
Narrows to the conversations waiting in one team's queue — the inbox's queue tabs. A chat matches while its open
connection is queued for that team (`ChatSummary.queue_group_id`);
the team that merely grants access to it (`group_id`) is a different
question. Composes with `view` and `channel`, and `total` counts the
same intersection.

parameters.name: priority
parameters.description:
Narrows to the chats whose open connection has this priority
(AI-12 · `ChatSummary.priority`) — an archived chat has none and
never matches. Composes with the other filters, and `total` counts
the same intersection.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description:
Words to find in message text (see above). Surrounding and repeated
whitespace is ignored.

parameters.name: date_from
parameters.description: With `query`, the earliest message time searched (inclusive).

parameters.name: date_to
parameters.description: With `query`, the end of the searched range (exclusive).

total.description:
Matching the current view, across all pages — the same
envelope `/tickets` and `/customers` return.

It is a field on the list rather than a separate count
endpoint because the number and the rows have to describe
the same instant: both are read inside one tenant
transaction, so a chat closing between them cannot make the
counter disagree with the list beside it. A second endpoint
would also double the console's rail from seven requests to
fourteen — the sidebar mounts one list per view.

For `ai_solved` this is the AI-resolution count, so
it is the same predicate the invoice meters. Counting the
rows the browser happened to load instead — the console did,
up to `limit` — is silently wrong from the 51st resolution
on, and gets quieter the larger the workspace.

waiting_thresholds.description:
The seconds after which a row's waiting counter turns to a
warning and to an alert: the workspace's setting
for the active brand (`/settings/chat-timeout`), else 120
and 300. Sent with the list because the settings endpoint
is the admins' and every agent's inbox draws the counter.

post.summary: Start a conversation with a customer
post.description:
Reuses the customer's existing active chat if there is one — a second
active chat for the same person is refused by the database, and silently
returning the existing one is what the caller almost always wants.

Otherwise the conversation opens in the customer's day: a chat
is one customer's day, so if the customer already has a chat for today
it gains a further connection (`opened_via: agent_start`) and is
returned with the same `id`; only the day's first connection creates a
chat. The connection's team joins the chat's `access` without removing
any. An active chat left over from an earlier day and silent for longer
than the workspace's idle window is closed at the turn of the day
(`day_rollover`), exactly as the visitor's next message would close it.

group_ids.description: Teams granted access. Defaults to the routing fallback.

assign_to_me.description:
Give the opened connection to the caller rather than to
routing. A teammate whose `initial_event` is addressed to the
customer (`recipients: all`, the default) is given it whatever
this says: only the assigned agent writes to the customer
(`sendEvent`), so the agent who opens a conversation by
writing to the customer has it.

initial_event.description:
The connection's opening line, written as the caller. Addressed
to the customer, from a teammate, it assigns the connection to
them (see `assign_to_me`); an internal note
(`recipients: agents`) leaves the assignment to `assign_to_me`.

200.description: An active chat already existed and was returned unchanged

201.description:
A connection was opened — a new chat for the customer's day, or a
further connection under the day's existing chat (same `id`).

get.summary: Fetch one conversation with its current thread
get.description:
`thread` is the newest connection; `connections` lists the day's
connections oldest first so a reader can draw the whole day and
fetch each transcript by `thread_id`.

Ordered oldest-first within a thread by default. `after_event_id` replays
everything since a known event — the same primitive the realtime layer
uses to recover missed messages after a reconnect.

A transcript that opens at the newest message and loads history as the
reader scrolls up asks the opposite question, so `sort: newest` answers
it: the tail of the thread first, then `before_event_id` walks backwards
a page at a time. Both directions page on the sequence embedded in the
event id rather than on `created_at`, because several events can share a
millisecond and an offset page shifts under an active conversation.

`next_page_id` is always the id of the last item returned: feed it back
as `after_event_id` when sorting oldest-first and as `before_event_id`
when sorting newest-first.

Internal notes are included for agents and omitted for customers.

parameters.name: thread_id
parameters.description:
Which connection's transcript to read — any id `Chat.connections`
lists (Panelde: Chat ID, bağlantı). Defaults to the most recent
thread. A thread of another chat is `404`, never a way into it.

parameters.name: after_event_id
parameters.description: Return only events following this one, in the same thread.

parameters.name: before_event_id
parameters.description: Return only events preceding this one, in the same thread.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description:
`oldest` — ascending from the start of the thread (the default, and
what a replay wants) · `newest` — descending from the end of it,
which is what a transcript that scrolls backwards wants.

post.summary: Send a message, internal note or system event
post.description:
Idempotent when `idempotency_key` is supplied: retrying after a timeout
returns the original event rather than posting a duplicate. Without it, a
flaky connection turns one message into several.

Refuses to write to a closed conversation (`chat_inactive`) — resume it
first, which starts a new thread.

**A reply to the customer comes only from the assigned agent**.
A teammate's event the customer sees (`recipients: all`) is written only
when the conversation's open connection is assigned to them; anyone else
receives `409 reply_requires_assignment` with
`ReplyRequiresAssignmentDetails` as `details` — `assigned_to_other`
(another teammate has it), `ai` (nobody has it and the AI is answering
it or is held back) or `unassigned` (nobody has it). Nothing is written
then: no event, no change to who answers the conversation, no delivery
to the customer's channel, and an `idempotency_key` sent with it is not
used up. Take the conversation first (`POST /chats/{chatId}/claim`, or
`POST /chats/{chatId}/takeover` for a colleague's), or have it assigned.
An internal note (`recipients: agents`) is never refused: any teammate
who can see the conversation writes one. A bot token is not subject to
the rule.

The check reads the connection under its row lock — the lock a takeover,
a "Take" and every other re-assignment also take — so a reply is never
written after the conversation moved on: it went out while the
conversation was still the sender's, or it is refused. Two teammates'
replies never both reach the customer.

200.description: Replay of an idempotent request; the original event

409.description:
The conversation is not active (`chat_inactive`), or a message to the
customer from a teammate it is not assigned to
(`reply_requires_assignment`)

put.summary: Correct a message after it was sent
put.description:
Rewrites the text of a message the caller sent themselves, within
fifteen minutes of sending it. The
corrected text replaces the original **in place**: the requirement is
that the wrong sentence stops being readable, so a correction that left
the original quoted in reports, exports and the transcript e-mail would
not meet it.

Nothing about the event log's shape changes. No event is deleted, no id
is reused and no sequence number moves, so `after_event_id` and the
realtime replay still have exactly one answer. Subscribers are told
through the `event_updated` push, which carries the whole event rather
than a diff.

`audit_log` records `chat.message_edited` — actor, chat and event id,
never the retracted text. The old wording is not retained anywhere; that
is the point of the operation.

Refused (403 `not_allowed`, with `details.reason`) when the caller did
not write the message (`not_author`), when the fifteen minutes have
passed (`edit_window_expired`), when the event is not a plain message
(`not_editable_type`), or when the reply has already been handed to an
external channel (`channel_delivered`) — a message delivered as an SMS or
a Messenger reply cannot be recalled from the provider, and rewriting the
local transcript would make our record disagree with what the customer
actually received.

parameters.name: eventId
parameters.description: `<thread_id>_<sequence>`, as returned by the send.

200.description: The event, carrying its new text and its `edited_at` marker

post.description:
Archives the conversation. The chat itself persists so the customer's
history stays intact and `resume` can continue it.

Opens a **new thread** (`opened_via: agent_reopen`), assigned to the
caller, rather than reviving the closed one, so the archived exchange
stays exactly as it was.

Where the new thread goes depends on the conversation's day. A chat filed under today — or under no day, a chat opened
before the daily model — is reopened in place. A chat filed under an
**earlier day** is not: a day that has ended gains no connection, so the
conversation continues under the customer's chat for today (found, or
opened), and the response is **that** chat — a different `id` the
caller should move to. The new thread's opening event ("Chat reopened")
carries `properties.continued_from_chat_id` naming the chat that was
reopened, and the reopened chat's teams join today's `access`.

200.description:
Reopened, with a new active thread — the requested chat, or, for an
earlier day's chat, the customer's chat for today.

409.description: Already active, or the customer already has another active chat

post.summary: Hand the conversation to another team or agent
post.description:
A hand-off to a team replaces the chat's `access` with that team and
records it as the open connection's `group_id`; a hand-off to an agent
changes neither. (A customer returning the same day adds a team instead
— ID-02-S7 — because a return is not a hand-off.)

A hand-off to a team gives the conversation to one of its members by
the usual routing order (`outcome: assigned`) — not the caller, nor the
agent who held it — and with nobody free it waits in that team's queue
(`outcome: queued`) for the next member who is; it is
never refused for being unstaffed, and never overflows to the fallback
team. A team with no members at all is a 409 `group_unavailable`. A
`note` is written into the conversation as a line only agents see; a
person handing to the Responsible Gambling or the Complaints team must
give one (IN-04-S2, 400 `validation`). A queued hand-off to the
Responsible Gambling team is also announced to the workspace's
supervisors. `visible_to_caller` says whether the caller can still open
the conversation: a team hand-off narrows its access to the receiving
team.

note.description:
What the receiving side should know, written as an internal
note (`recipients: agents`) — never shown to the customer.

reason.description:
Who handed the conversation over. `ai_handoff` is the AI
Agent's and is what the AI report attributes a transfer to;
`bot_handoff` is the deterministic rule bot's,
separate so a rule firing never reads as a model deciding.
`agent_unresponsive` is the inactivity sweep's: the
assigned agent did not answer within
`unanswered_transfer_seconds`.

409.description:
The chat is closed (`chat_inactive`), the target agent is offline or
the target team has no members (`group_unavailable`)

get.description:
One connection's transcript as a file, streamed:
`txt` (plain text) or `html` (a printable page — the browser's "Save
as PDF" keeps every Turkish letter). Headed with the workspace, the
Thread ID (`chat_id`) and the Chat ID (`thread_id`), the player's
username, the start and end in the workspace's time zone, the agents,
and who exported it when. A file is listed by its name with a note to
open it in the panel — no link to it.

`audience=customer` is the player's copy: no internal note.
`audience=internal` carries them, marked as notes.

Who may: the permission matrix's `transcripts.export`, inside
`chats.view` (AR-04-S1, Ekip Lideri and up by default): `own` — a
connection the person was assigned, wrote on or joined; `team` — one
routed to a team of theirs; `all` — any they may see. A role at `none`
is `403` `capability_required`; a chat or connection outside the reach,
or another workspace's, is `404`. At most 10 downloads,
prints and mails a person a minute (`429`). Every download writes
`chat.transcript_exported` (format and copy, no text) to the audit log
before the first byte.

Agents only.

parameters.name: threadId
parameters.description: One connection of the day (Panelde: Chat ID).

post.description: Tags describe a thread, not a chat — what a conversation is about can change between visits.

delete.summary: Remove a tag from the current thread

post.summary: Record how far the caller has read

get.description:
Ordered by `sort` + `order` over the **whole** collection, not the page —
the default is most recent activity first, which is what a support team
actually scans for. Paginated by opaque keyset cursor rather than offset —
with new conversations arriving constantly an offset page shifts under the
reader and silently skips people.

**`page_id` belongs to one sort.** The cursor carries the value of the
sorted column of the last row on the previous page, so it means nothing
under a different `sort`/`order` — presenting one issued under another
ordering is a `400` rather than a silent restart from page one.

Anonymous visitors are included: someone who opened the widget and never
gave a name is still a person waiting for an answer. They surface with a
null name rather than being filtered away.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: Case-insensitive match against name, email and phone (anywhere in the text) and the pre-chat username (from its start). Email and username are matched only for a caller whose role may see a player's contact details (`customers.contact.view`).

parameters.name: segment
parameters.description:
`all` · `leads` — gave an email · `recent` — active in the last 30 days
· `banned`.

parameters.name: country_code
parameters.description:
Exact match against the customer's 2-letter country code (ISO
3166-1 alpha-2), upper-cased before comparison.

parameters.name: last_activity_from
parameters.description: Only customers active on or after this date (inclusive, UTC).

parameters.name: last_activity_to
parameters.description: Only customers active on or before this date (inclusive, UTC).

parameters.name: has_tickets
parameters.description:
`true` restricts to customers with at least one ticket in the
caller's license; `false` to those with none.

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description:
The column the whole collection is ordered by. `chats`/`tickets`
are deliberately absent: what the table shows is a count scoped to
the caller's license, and the database cannot order the whole
collection by that scoped number without disagreeing with the
cell it prints — see `CUSTOMER_SORT_KEYS` (`@siyahtus/types`). A
customer with no value in the sorted column (no name, no country)
sorts last in *both* directions, so an empty cell never outranks a
real one just because the order flipped.

total.description: Matching the current filter, across all pages.

get.description:
Includes recent visits and conversations. A customer in another tenant
returns 404, not 403 — a 403 would confirm the id is real.

patch.description:
Only the fields present in the body are changed, so two agents editing
different fields do not overwrite each other. Sending `null` clears a
field; omitting it leaves it alone.

get.summary: List tickets, newest activity first by default
get.description:
Ordered by `sort` + `order` over the **whole** collection, not over the
page. The default is `last_message` descending, which is the order the PRD
specifies and the order a queue is actually worked. Keyset pagination
rather than offset: tickets change status while someone is reading, and an
offset page shifts under them and skips rows.

`view` matches the PRD's Tickets group:

- `all` — everything the caller may see
- `unassigned` — no assignee; the pile nobody has picked up
- `my_open` — assigned to the caller and not yet solved or closed
- `solved` — solved or closed, the read-back pile

**`page_id` belongs to one sort.** The cursor is a position in a specific
ordering — it carries the value of the sorted column of the last row on the
previous page — so it means nothing under a different `sort` or `order`.
Presenting one that was issued under another ordering is a `400` rather
than a silent restart from page one, which would hand the caller rows they
already have and read as a second page.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: Case-insensitive match against subject and customer name/email (anywhere in the text), and the customer's pre-chat username (from its start). Email and username are matched only for a caller whose role may see a player's contact details (`customers.contact.view`).

parameters.name: sort
parameters.description:
The column the whole collection is ordered by. `customer` sorts on the
customer's name and `last_message` on the last activity; a ticket with
neither sorts last in *both* directions, because an empty cell should
never outrank a real one just because the order flipped.

The grid's `status` and `assignee` columns are absent on purpose:
`status` is stored as text (its lifecycle order — open before closed —
is not its alphabetical one) and a ticket holds only `assignee_id`,
while what is displayed and would be sorted on is the account's name.
The `view` parameter already slices the collection by both.

`sla` orders by `sla.first_response_due_at` — `asc` puts the
ticket nearest its first-response target first; a ticket whose clock
is not running sorts last in both directions.

total.description: Matching the current view, across all pages.

post.summary: Create a ticket, optionally from a chat
post.description:
Two ways in. From a chat (`source_chat_id`) — the PRD's "Create ticket"
action, which carries the customer across so the follow-up is attached to
the same person. Or standalone with a `customer_id`, which is how an
inbound email becomes a ticket.

**A chat gets at most one unresolved ticket.** An agent who clicks the
button twice, or two agents looking at the same conversation, would
otherwise split the follow-up across two tickets and one of them would be
forgotten. A second attempt returns `409` with the existing id so the
client can open it instead. The rule is a partial unique index, not an
application check, so a race cannot slip between the two.

source_chat_id.description: The chat this follows up on. Supplies the customer if `customer_id` is omitted.

409.description:
The chat already has an unresolved ticket. `details.existing_ticket_id`
carries it.

patch.summary: Change status, assignee, team or subject
patch.description:
Assigning to an agent outside the licence, or to a team that does not
exist, is refused rather than stored — a ticket pointing at nobody is a
ticket nobody works.

Solving a ticket does not delete it: `solved` and `closed` stay readable
in the `solved` view.

`email_template_id` tells the customer what happened, in the workspace's
own words. It names one of the templates
`/settings/ticket-email-templates` holds; its `{{ placeholders }}` are
filled from this ticket and the message is mailed to the customer once the
change is committed.

It is only accepted alongside a `status` that actually changes, because a
template may print `{{ticket.status}}` — a notice about a transition that
did not happen would state something untrue. It is refused, rather than
quietly skipped, when the template is disabled, when it holds a
placeholder the product cannot fill, or when the ticket has no customer
address to write to: the whole request fails and the status stays put, so
an agent is never told a customer was notified when nobody was.

put.summary: Set this ticket's custom field values
put.description:
A map of definition id → value, where null clears a field.
Each value is validated against its definition: a wrong type, or a blank on
a required field, is a 400. Returns the ticket, whose `custom_fields` now
carries the stored values.

200.description: The ticket, with its custom field values applied.

get.description:
Replies, internal notes, what the player wrote and the product's own
lines, oldest first — the order a conversation is read in.
Keyset pagination on `(created_at, id)`: `next_page_id` is present while
there is more, and is fed back as `page_id`.

A primary ticket's thread also carries the messages of the tickets merged
into it, interleaved by time; each item's `ticket_id` says where it was
written. A merged ticket's own thread still reads (it is history), but
writing to it is `409 ticket_merged`.

Visibility is the ticket's: a ticket the caller may not see — or one in
another tenant — is `404`, never `403`.

post.summary: Reply to the player, or add an internal note
post.description:
`kind: reply` stores the reply, then — after the commit — e-mails it to
the player from the system address under the brand's name, `[#<id>]` in
the subject, threaded on the previous message (`In-Reply-To` /
`References`). The response does not wait for the mail server:
`delivery_status` starts `queued` and the thread updates when it settles.
When this deployment keeps ticket e-mail off the reply is still
stored, with `delivery_status: suppressed`.

`kind: note` is for the team only and never reaches the mail path.

Without `set_status` a reply moves the ticket to `pending` (waiting on
the player); "send and solve" passes `set_status: solved`.

Retrying with the same `idempotency_key` returns the message stored the
first time (`200`) rather than a second one (`201`).

Refused with `409 ticket_merged` on a merged ticket
(`details.primary_ticket_id` names the one to write on), and with
`409 ticket_no_recipient` for a reply to a player who left no e-mail
address — a note is still allowed. A ticket the caller may not see, or
one in another tenant, is `404`.

200.description: The same `idempotency_key` was seen before; the message it stored.

409.description:
`ticket_merged` — the ticket was merged; `details.primary_ticket_id`
is where its conversation continues. `ticket_no_recipient` — a reply
to a player with no e-mail address.

post.description:
Blocks new conversations and refuses to mint further widget tokens for
them. Existing history is kept: a ban is a moderation decision, not a
deletion request, and erasing the record would also erase the evidence
for it.

Requires `customers.ban:rw` — separate from ordinary customer editing
because it is the one customer action that denies someone service.

put.summary: Set this contact's custom field values
put.description:
A map of definition id → value, where null clears a field.
Each value is validated against its definition: a wrong type, or a blank on
a required field, is a 400. Returns the contact, whose `custom_fields` now
carries the stored values.

200.description: The contact, with its custom field values applied.

get.description:
Defaults to the active roster: suspended agents are omitted, because they
cannot be assigned work and offering them in an assignee picker only
produces a failed transfer.

Pass `status=suspended` for the Suspended tab, or
`status=all` to see everyone regardless of state. Each item carries a
`suspended` flag so a combined list can be split client-side.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Which slice of the roster to return.

get.description:
Teams are the unit of chat visibility: an agent sees a conversation because
a team they belong to has access to it. Membership carries the priority
that routing uses to pick between available agents.

get.summary: List past conversations, one row per connection
get.description:
The archive screen's list. A row is one **connection** — panel
"Chat ID", `thread_id` — not a day: a player who wrote three times is
three rows, each with its own tags, assignee and rating. `chat_id` is the
day the connection belongs to (panel "Thread ID"); a reopened
conversation is a new connection and leaves the earlier one here as it
was.

Closed connections by default, the most recently ended first
(`status=closed`). `status=all` puts the connections still open first,
then the closed ones; `status=open` lists only those.

What the caller may see is part of the query, not a filter applied to a
page afterwards: a Team Member and a Team Lead see the conversations of
their teams and the ones they took part in, a Manager and the Founder
every one. A connection past the workspace's retention window is
not listed — the sweep deletes it — and a member who was erased has no
rows at all.

Not live: no push keeps the list current, and nothing here writes.
Searching by number or by message text is `GET /search` and
`GET /chats?query=`; their results carry the `thread_id` that is a row
here.

**Filters.** Different filters combine with AND, the values of
one filter with OR (`agent_id=a&agent_id=b` is "a or b"); tags combine
as `tag_mode` says. `total` counts the filtered list. Every filter
carries ids, never a name or an e-mail address, so a filtered address
can be shared without carrying anyone's personal data. Filters that
cannot both hold (`untagged` with `tag_mode=any`, `handled_by=ai` with
an agent) are applied as asked and give an empty list; the screen warns.

parameters.name: customer_id
parameters.description: One member's connections — the player card's "All".

parameters.name: date_from
parameters.description:
The first conversation day, `YYYY-MM-DD`, on the workspace's own
calendar — the zone and start hour of its conversation day,
not UTC. A connection is in the range by when it **started**: at or after the first instant of `date_from`, before the
first instant of the day after `date_to`. Either end may be left
open. Not together with `from`/`to` (400 `reason: date_mixed`); a
`date_to` before `date_from` is 400 `reason: range_order`.

parameters.name: date_to
parameters.description: The last conversation day, `YYYY-MM-DD`, included. See `date_from`.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description:
Connections that started at or after this instant — the exact-time
form of `date_from`, for a range that is not whole days.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Connections that started before this instant (excluded).

parameters.name: agent_id
parameters.description:
Connections one of these agents wrote in to the player — internal
notes do not count — repeated once per agent. Recorded as the
connection closes (`threads.agent_ids`); an open one is read live.

parameters.name: group_id
parameters.description:
Connections of these teams — the team a connection went to, and for
one opened before that was recorded, the teams its day was given:
the same teams the row's `group_ids` lists.

parameters.name: rating
parameters.description:
The connection's **newest** rating — the one the row shows. `any`:
rated; `not_rated`: never rated; `commented`: a rating with a
comment, either value.

parameters.name: tag
parameters.description: Tags, repeated once per tag, at most 20. How they combine is `tag_mode`.

parameters.name: tag_mode
parameters.description:
`any` — at least one of the tags; `all` — every one of them;
`exclude` — none of them (an untagged connection is kept).

parameters.name: untagged
parameters.description: `true`: only connections with no tag at all.

parameters.name: handled_by
parameters.description:
Who answered it (`ArchiveConversation.handled_by`). `ai` is "AI
solved": the invoice's AI resolution, so its count over a
range is the AI report's `resolutions` for the same range.

parameters.name: risk_flag
parameters.description: Connections where one of these risk flags was raised, cleared ones included.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description:
Connections of the days that arrived over one messaging channel — the
inbox's definition (`GET /chats?channel=`): the channel of the day's
oldest inbound adapter message.

200.description:
One page. `total` counts the whole list up to 1 000; past that
`total_capped` is true and the count stops there.

get.description:
The archive's detail for one connection: its row, the rating with its
comment, and its summary. The tags, the assignee and the rating are
this connection's — never the day's newest connection's. The transcript
is `GET /chats/{chat_id}/events?thread_id=`.

A connection the caller may not see, of another workspace, or erased is
a 404. So is one past the workspace's retention window, with
`error.details.reason: retention_expired` — its transcript is deleted
or about to be.

parameters.name: threadId
parameters.description: The connection. Panelde: Chat ID.

get.description:
Every brand of the caller's license, the default brand first. A
single-brand workspace sees exactly one row — the `Default` brand every
license is created with.

404.description: No such brand in this license (`brand_not_found`)

get.summary: Sites the widget is installed on
One website, with its install snippet

get.description:
Never includes the signing secret — that is shown only once, when the
webhook is registered.

post.description:
The `url` must be a public `http(s)` address; a private, loopback or
link-local target is rejected at registration (SSRF, NFR-S7), and checked
again at delivery in case DNS changes underneath it.

A refused `url` carries `error.details.reason`: `url_invalid`,
`url_scheme`, `url_credentials` or `url_private_host`. A refused `app_id`
carries `app_not_automation` or `app_not_connected` (with `app_name`).

The response carries the signing `secret` **once**. Store it: every
delivery is signed `HMAC-SHA256(secret, "{timestamp}.{nonce}.{body}")` in
the `X-Webhook-Signature` header, and there is no way to retrieve the
secret again — a lost secret means deleting and re-registering.

url.description: Public http(s) endpoint that receives the POST.

type.description:
`license` for a workspace integration, `bot` for one scoped to
a single bot client. Defaults to `license`.

app_id.description:
Attach this subscription to a connected automation card — `zapier` or `make`. This is the Zapier REST
Hooks leg: a zap's catch hook is registered here like any
other subscriber, and the card then reports how many triggers
it owns and when one last fired.

Two refusals, both 400: the id must name an automation card
(no other kind of app may own a subscription), and that card
must already be connected in this workspace. Disconnecting it
removes every subscription registered this way, so a
workspace event cannot reach an integration nobody agreed to.

Omit it for an ordinary webhook — the default, and what every
subscription registered before 09.4 is.

201.description: Registered — the secret is present on this response only

patch.summary: Switch a webhook on or off
patch.description:
Only `enabled` can change: a switched-off webhook receives no new
events, and a delivery still queued for it is given up rather than sent
(consent withdrawn). The URL, event and secret are fixed at registration —
to change one, register a new webhook.

200.description: The webhook as it is now

delete.description:
Stops all future deliveries to this endpoint. Past delivery log entries
are removed with it.

get.summary: The delivery log of one webhook
get.description:
One row per **attempt**, newest first, by `next_cursor`. A row
says what happened to one send: the HTTP status the receiver answered
with and a short, cleaned error (`http_503`, `ssrf_blocked`,
`ECONNREFUSED`, `AbortError` — never a response body, a URL or a secret;
at most 500 characters).

`state` filters: `pending` (another try is queued), `delivered`,
`failed` (an attempt a later one superseded) or `exhausted` (gave up).
`can_redeliver` says whether "Redeliver" would work on the row — the
payload of an exhausted delivery is kept 72 hours, a delivered one is
never kept.

post.description:
Re-sends the stored payload of a queued or exhausted delivery through the
normal sender — the SSRF check, the signature and a fresh nonce included —
and returns the **new attempt row**, which is also the newest row of the
log. The row it replaces becomes `failed` (superseded).

A refused redelivery is a `400` validation error whose
`error.details.reason` is `not_redeliverable` (a delivered attempt, a test
ping, a row whose payload has aged out, or one that is no longer the
newest attempt) or `webhook_disabled`.

POSTs a signed ping to the webhook — `{"action": …, "test": true, "data":
{…}}` with the same headers a real delivery carries — and returns what the
receiver answered. The attempt is logged with `test: true`, is never
queued for a retry, and does not count toward an automation card's "last
run". Works on a switched-off webhook too (check it before switching on).
A few per minute per webhook; `429` beyond that.

post.summary: Ask permission to upload an attachment
post.description:
The rules from `security_settings` are enforced here,
before any bytes move: file sharing switched off, a type outside
`allowed_file_types`, or a size above `max_file_size_bytes` all fail at
this step and no URL is issued. A grant that never exists is a file that
can never be stored, which is why this is the enforcement point rather
than the PUT alone.

The returned `upload_url` carries its own signature and is good for one
file of exactly the declared type and length, for `UPLOAD_URL_TTL`
seconds. `file_url` is what belongs on the event as `attachment_url`; it
does not expire and is authorised by session instead.

**`purpose: knowledge_document`** asks for a PDF or Word
document for the knowledge base instead. The conversation's file-sharing
rules do not apply to it — they govern what a chat may carry; this is
the knowledge editor's own upload, so it needs the
`agents-bot--all:rw` scope, and a customer or a member without that
scope is refused (403). Only `application/pdf` and the DOCX type are
granted (400, `details.reason` `unsupported_type`), up to 20 MiB (400,
`file_too_large`). The grant carries `upload_id` and no `file_url`: the
document is stored under a key `GET /uploads/{key}` never serves, and
`POST /knowledge-sources/document` is what takes `upload_id`.

filename.description:
Advisory only. The stored key is `<licence>/<uuid><ext>` with
the extension rebuilt from `content_type`; the supplied name
never becomes a path segment.

purpose.description:
`attachment` — a file in a conversation (the default);
`knowledge_document` — a PDF or DOCX for the knowledge base.

400.description:
The type is not in `allowed_file_types`, or the size is above the
licence ceiling. `details` carries the rule that refused it. For a
`knowledge_document`, `details.reason` is `unsupported_type` or
`file_too_large`.

403.description:
File sharing is switched off for this licence; or, for a
`knowledge_document`, the caller is not a member holding
`agents-bot--all:rw`.

get.summary: Whether file sharing is on for this licence
get.description:
Just the on/off switch from `security_settings` — not the
allowed types or size ceiling, which stay server-only (a client-side
pre-check of those would only duplicate what `POST /uploads` already
refuses). Reachable by every agent role, unlike `GET /settings/security`
(`access_rules:ro`, admin-only): the composer needs this to decide
whether to show the attachment button at all, before the agent has
picked a file and hit the refusal.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The opaque `<licence>/<uuid><ext>` key from the grant.

get.description:
Authorised by session, and the licence inside the key has to match the
caller's. A key belonging to another licence answers `404`, not `403`:
whether it exists is not something this caller gets to learn.

Served as `content-disposition: attachment` with `nosniff`. An allowed
`text/plain` rendered inline in our own origin would be stored XSS given
away for free.

A knowledge document's key (`purpose: knowledge_document`) is not an
attachment and answers `404` here, for every caller: its original is
reached only through `GET /knowledge-sources/{sourceId}/file`.

put.summary: Send the bytes for a granted upload
put.description:
Authorised by the signature in the query string, not by a session — it is
narrower than one: a single key, type and length, inside a short window.
The declared type and length are compared against what the request
actually carries, so a grant for a small PNG cannot deliver a large
anything-else.

Every rejection answers the same way. Telling a caller which part of a
forgery failed is how a forgery gets refined.

The bytes are virus-scanned before anything is stored; a scanner that
cannot be reached refuses the upload (503) rather than storing it
unscanned. A `knowledge_document`'s type is then read from its bytes —
`%PDF-` at the first byte, or a ZIP listing `word/document.xml` and no
VBA project — and must be the type the grant was for: anything else
(a renamed executable, a `.docm`) is a 400 with `details.reason`
`unsupported_type`, and nothing is stored.

file_url.description: Where an attachment is readable; absent for a `knowledge_document`.

400.description:
The virus scan refused the file (`details.reason` `virus_detected`),
or a `knowledge_document`'s bytes are not the document type granted
(`unsupported_type`). Nothing was stored.

403.description: The URL is expired, forged, or does not match the bytes sent

503.description: The virus scanner could not be reached; nothing was stored.

NotificationPreferences.description:
Every channel the product can reach one person through, for one
workspace.

`enabled` is a master switch over the *interruptive* channels — `sound`,
`desktop`, `push` — and deliberately not over `email`. Those three
announce something now; e-mail is the fallback for somebody who is not
at a screen at all, and "stop interrupting me" was never a request to
stop the fallback as well.

All five default to on. The failure this product cannot afford is an
agent who never learns a visitor is waiting, so a new member is
reachable and opts out rather than in.

`events` is the other half of the question: which things are
worth an interruption at all. `incoming_chat` — a visitor wrote in — is
always `true`; what a person can silence is its *sound* (the `sound`
channel). `repeat_sound` keeps the chime going every 10 seconds until the
message is read; it defaults to off.

digest_daily.description:
Whether the daily summary e-mail reaches this person: their own
choice, or while they have made none the workspace default for their
role (`GET /settings/digests`). Gated by `email` like every other mail.

digest_weekly.description: The same for the weekly summary, each Monday.

NotificationEvents.description:
Which events interrupt one person. Every key is always
present in a response; a key a stored object lacks reads as its default
(`queue_waiting` off, the rest on). `incoming_chat` cannot be turned off.

transferred_to_me.description: A chat was handed to you.

transferred_to_my_team.description: A chat was handed to a team you are in.

queue_waiting.description: A visitor is waiting in a queue of a team you are in.

new_ticket.description: A ticket was opened or assigned to you or your team.

ticket_reply.description: The player answered a ticket you work.

PanelAppearance.description:
What the panel paints, resolved on the server: the later of the
workspace default and the caller's own choice, or the built-in Inter
when neither exists. Both layers ride along so the account menu can
say where the font comes from.

Health.description:
`status` + `service` are always present. Every other field is
admin-only — absent for an anonymous or non-admin caller,
present together for an admin-role one.

status.description:
`ok` every dependency is reachable · `degraded` at least one is not
(503) · `draining` the process is shutting down and has taken
itself out of rotation on purpose (503, M-OPS-b). The last two share
a status code because an orchestrator should stop routing either
way, and are told apart here because the responses a human owes them
are opposite ones.

ai_jobs.description: Null when the queue could not be read.

SchedulerHealth.description:
The in-process background scheduler — idle-chat
auto-close, SLA breach marking, the SIEM export, scheduled reports and
retention. `enabled` false means this process runs none of them (every
job below is still listed, each `disabled`); a deployment that would
rather drive the sweeps from a host cron leaves it off and uses each
job's own `pnpm --filter @siyahtus/api <job>:run` script instead.

enabled.description:
False for a job registered but switched off from the moment it was
registered — `retention`, gated by `RETENTION_ENABLED` because it
hard-deletes data, and `unverified_signups`, which runs only while
`SIGNUP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION` is on: with it off an unverified account
signs in like any other, so there is nothing to delete it for.

last_run_at.description: When the job last ticked, whatever came of it. Null before its first pass.

last_error_class.description: The error's class, never its message — driver messages can carry connection strings.

EventPartitionsHealth.description:
The `events` monthly partition maintenance (SEMA-MIMARI.8.4c · PLAN
§D187). Not a scheduler job: every API process runs it at boot and
every `interval_ms`, whatever `SCHEDULER_ENABLED` says, opening each
month from `months_behind` before the current one to `months_ahead`
after it. A month that has no partition when its first event arrives
sends every event of that month to the unindexed `events_default`
catch-all, so a failing pass is worth noticing three months early —
which is what this block is for. It never changes the status code:
the process still serves, and restarting it fixes nothing.

last_run_at.description: When the last pass finished, whatever came of it. Null only before the boot pass.

last_status.description: `error` when at least one month of the last pass failed.

consecutive_errors.description: Failed passes in a row; back to 0 on the first clean one.

failed_months.description: The months the last pass could not open or secure. Empty when it was clean.

error_code.description:
The SQLSTATE the database answered with — `42501` the
runtime role lacks the owner's rights (the maintenance
functions lost SECURITY DEFINER), `23514` rows for that
month already sit in `events_default` (the owner releases
them — `docs/runbooks/event-partitions.md`), `55P03` a lock
was not free within a second (retried next pass). When the
database never answered, the error's class. Never the
message.

AiJobsHealth.description:
The durable AI job queue, across every
workspace: the replies visitor messages are still owed. A queue that
grows, or whose oldest job keeps ageing, means no worker is taking
jobs; past 120 s a job is handed to a person instead of answered.
Body only, never the status code.

pending.description: Jobs waiting for a worker, those handed back for a retry included.

running.description: Jobs a worker holds right now.

oldest_age_s.description:
Seconds since the oldest unfinished (`pending` or `running`) job
was written, by the database's clock. Null when there is none.

HealthProviders.description:
Which implementation each mockable dependency
currently runs, read straight off the validated environment — so an
operator can tell "mail is really SMTP" from "mail writes to disk"
without reading `.env` on the box. Every dependency here is mocked or
file-backed by default (MASTER-PROMPT "dış servisler mock'lanır");
none of these becoming a real provider changes this endpoint's shape.

ImpersonationState.description:
A SiyahTuş operator signed in as this member from the root panel. Who the operator is stays in the audit
trail (`actor_type: platform`); the console needs only the terms.

mode.description:
`read_only` refuses every write but signing out and ending the
session; `full` acts as the member. Neither reaches past the
member's role.

ends_at.description: When the session, and every token traded for it, stops working.

id.description:
Short base32 token, e.g. TJ1H8CFKRV. Panelde: Thread ID (günlük) —
the member's conversation container for the day; every connection
(`Thread`) of that day sits under it. The field name does not change;
only the panel's label does (docs/adr/conversation-day-ids.md).

thread.description: The newest connection — the open one while the chat is active.

local_day.description:
The conversation day this chat is filed under (`YYYY-MM-DD`, ID-02):
one chat per member per day, counted in the workspace's day
boundary (`day_boundary_timezone` / `day_boundary_hour` of
`/settings/chat-timeout`) as it stood when the chat opened. Written
once and never recomputed, so a later change of the setting does
not move it. Null for a chat that is not filed under a day — every
chat opened before the daily model; such a chat spans the whole
relationship rather than one day.

connections.description:
The connections (`Thread`s, "Panelde: Chat ID") this chat holds
for its day, oldest first; read any one's transcript with
`GET /chats/{chatId}/events?thread_id=`. A chat with a `local_day`
lists every connection of that day. A chat without one lists only
its newest connection: it is not a day, and its older threads are
earlier visits rather than today's connections.

latest_ai_handoff.description:
The newest card the AI wrote in this chat — on the agent's
fetch of a single chat (`GET /chats/{chatId}`) only; null when the AI
handed nothing over. Never on the customer's view.

visitor.description:
The customer's most recent visit for this license, projected onto
the chat so the Details panel can show where the visitor came from
without a second call. Null when nothing was recorded,
and omitted entirely on the customer's own view — the IP in
particular is personal data the widget never receives.

ChatTransferResult.description:
The chat after a hand-off (`POST /chats/{chatId}/transfer`), with what
became of it.

outcome.description:
`assigned` — someone has it (the named agent, or a member of
the team); `queued` — nobody in the team was free, so it waits
in that team's queue for the next member who is.

visible_to_caller.description:
Whether the caller can still open the conversation. False after
a team hand-off by someone outside the receiving team who never
joined the conversation: the console moves on instead of
re-reading a chat it would be refused.

id.description: Panelde: Thread ID (günlük) — the same `chat_id` token as `Chat.id`.

thread_id.description: Panelde: Chat ID (bağlantı) — the most recent connection of this day.

queue_group_id.description:
The team whose queue the newest connection waits in — null while it waits in none (`queue_position`
null). The `queue_position` is that team's number.

priority.description: How pressing the newest connection is; `normal` for a chat with none.

inactive.description:
The newest connection is open and inactive: quiet for the
workspace's `inactive_after_seconds`, so it does not count against
its agent's concurrent limit until the next message. The inbox
shows the row dimmed. False for a closed or a lively one.

waiting_since.description:
Since when the player has waited for an answer: the first
player message nobody has answered, or the moment the AI handed
the player to a person. Cleared by an agent's or a bot's reply the
player sees and by the close; an internal note or a "chat
transferred" line leaves it. Null: nobody waits (and for a closed
chat). The one source of the inbox row's counter.

queued_at.description:
When the newest connection joined its team's queue; null while it
waits in none (`queue_position` null). The counter for a queued row.

connection_count.description:
How many connections `Chat.connections` lists for this chat — the
day's connections when the chat has a `local_day`, otherwise at most
one (its newest). The list row's "N connections".

match.description:
Present only on a text search (`GET /chats?query=`, ID-07): the
message this conversation was found by.

MessageSearchMatch.description: A conversation's newest message containing every word of the query. `created_at` is to the millisecond.

snippet.description:
The message around its first match: up to 60 characters either
side, `…` where the text was cut.

highlights.description: Where the query's words sit in `snippet` — character ranges, in order, never overlapping.

match_count.description: Matching messages in the conversation, this one included.

internal.description: The message is an internal note, which the visitor never saw.

TextRange.description: A character range `[start, end)` (UTF-16 code units, as JavaScript indexes a string).

chat_id.description: Panelde: Thread ID (günlük) — the day container this connection sits under.

opened_via.description: How this connection came to exist; null on a thread opened before ID-02.

ai_mode.description:
Who answers the connection. `ai`: the AI agent; `human`: a
person has it and the AI stays silent; `paused`: the AI is held
back without a person having taken it. Null until the AI or a
person takes part — the AI may still answer. Changes are pushed to
agents as `chat_ai_mode_changed`.

waiting_since.description:
Since when the player has waited for an answer: the first
player message nobody has answered, or the moment the AI handed
the player to a person. Cleared by an agent's or a bot's reply the
player sees and by the close; an internal note or a "chat
transferred" line leaves it. Null: nobody waits (and for a closed
chat). The one source of the inbox row's counter.

queued_at.description:
When the newest connection joined its team's queue; null while it
waits in none (`queue_position` null). The counter for a queued row.

priority.description:
How pressing the connection is; `normal`
until a hand-over or a route raises it. Never lowered.

priority_reason.description:
The hand-over reason (a catalogue code such as
`guardrail_self_harm`) that last raised `priority`; null while
nothing has.

ai_took_part.description:
Whether the AI has answered in this connection — what tells a
`human` connection the AI was taken off from one a person answered
from the start. Present only on the agent's fetch of a single chat
(`GET /chats/{chatId}`).

rating.description:
The player's rating of this connection, with its
comment. Null when it is not rated, or when the caller may not see
it (`ratings.view`: an Ekip Üyesi reads the ratings of their own
connections). Present only on the agent's fetch of a single chat
(`GET /chats/{chatId}`); a change is pushed as `chat_rated`.

comment.description: Plain text as the player wrote it, sensitive values masked.

ChatConnection.description:
One connection of a chat's day, as `Chat.connections` lists it —
enough to draw the separators between connections and to fetch each
transcript, without the transcript itself.

id.description: Panelde: Chat ID (bağlantı) — the `thread_id` to read its events with.

group_id.description:
The team this connection went to: the one routing chose, the one
it was opened in, or the one a transfer handed it to. Null when it
went to no single team (none, or several named at once) and on a
connection opened before the team was recorded. The chat's
`access` is the union over its connections — a team that handled
one connection of the day reads the whole day.

ConnectionOpenedVia.description:
How a connection (`thread`) came to exist:
`first_of_day` — the member's first connection of the day, which opens
the day's chat · `same_day_return` — the member came back the same day,
a new connection under the same chat · `agent_start` — an agent started
the conversation · `agent_reopen` — an agent reopened an archived
conversation · `day_rollover` — opened as yesterday's silent connection
was closed at the turn of the day. Null (on `Thread` and
`ChatConnection`) for a connection opened before ID-02.

ChatVisitor.description:
A visit projected onto the chat surface: the pages the
visitor saw and a short summary of the session.

visited_pages.description: Pages seen during the visit, in order.

device.description: Browser and operating system, e.g. "Chrome on macOS".

referrer.description: Referring URL, when the browser sent one.

duration_seconds.description: Elapsed time of the visit in seconds; null if unknown.

ip.description: Visitor IP (NFR-S9 personal data; agents only).

country_code.description:
ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country the visit came from (GEOIP-COUNTRY ·
tm 330), resolved once at the visit's start from the address,
inside the API against an offline database. Null when no
database is configured or the address is not in it.

city.description: City the visit came from, on the same terms as `country_code`. No coordinates are kept.

ongoing.description:
True while the visit is still open (no recorded end). The PRD
asks for a live duration, and `duration_seconds` is only a
measurement taken when the response was written: a client may
tick it forward while this is true, and must not while it is
false — a finished visit has a fixed length, and a counter
climbing past it would be an invented number.

id.description: `<thread_id>_<sequence>` — ordering is decidable from the id alone.

recipients.description: `agents` is an internal note and never reaches the customer.

properties.description:
Free-form, with three reserved keys the server owns: `edited_at`
(ISO-8601, present once the message has been corrected after
sending), `edited_by` (the account that corrected it) and
`sensitive_types` (tm 300.2 · AI-26: the kinds of value masked out
of `text` before it was stored — `card`, `cvv`, `otp`, `password`,
`iban`, `seed_phrase`, `private_key`, `banking_credential` — in that
order). All three are stripped from a caller-supplied `properties`
on send, so a client cannot make a fresh message claim it was
edited or masked. The warning a visitor is shown after sharing a
secret is a `system_message` addressed to `all` with
`system_event: sensitive_data_warning`, once per chat per type; its
`sensitive_types` are the types it is the first warning for.

A `rich_message` carries its card as `card` (`RichCard`, EN-02)
and its plain text as `text`. A player's message sent by a card
button carries `postback` (`CardPostback`), which only the
server writes — it is stripped from a caller-supplied
`properties` too.

text.description:
The corrected wording. Replaces the original outright — there is no
partial edit, and an empty string is refused rather than treated as
a delete, which is a different operation with different rules.

properties.description:
A `rich_message` needs `properties.card` (`RichCard`).
In a conversation a card may only `send_message` or `open_url`
to one of the workspace's trusted domains — no `copy_coupon` —
whoever sends it (an agent, a bot, the AI); anything else is a 400
naming the button. Its `text` defaults to the card's plain text
(title, body, the buttons numbered), what a channel that cannot
draw a card sends.

idempotency_key.description: Retrying with the same key returns the original event.

RiskFlagType.description:
AI-27's flag types (`RISK_FLAG_TYPES`). The first three are the
player's as well as the conversation's.

AiHandoffCard.description:
The AI's hand-over card: built from the conversation's state
when the AI handed the connection to a person, never by a model. Its
`id` is the hand-over's `handoff_id`, which the transfer and AI-mode
events carry. `reason_codes`, `primary_reason` and `risk_flags` are
closed vocabularies of `@siyahtus/types` (`HANDOFF_REASONS`,
`RISK_FLAG_TYPES`). A `sensitive` slot was given and is kept off the
card (`text` null).

thread_id.description: Panelde: Chat ID (bağlantı) — the connection handed over.

topic.description: The procedure's name; null when no procedure ran.

summary.description:
One sentence: the procedure's name and what was collected, or
"Soru: <the player's first message>" when no procedure ran. Also
the connection's `Thread.summary`.

question.description: The player's question, on a hand-over no procedure ran.

username.description: Null when the caller's role may not see a player's contact details (`customers.contact.view`).

email.description: Null when the caller's role may not see a player's contact details (`customers.contact.view`).

basis.description: The player's own claim — not verified in F1.

recognized_device.description: A member token this workspace signed came with the message.

language.description:
The language the conversation was in (ISO 639-1, tm 387 · AI-30), as
the AI kept it; absent when not told. The card's own words are Turkish.

slots.description: The procedure's `show_in_card` slots, in its order, once there is something to say.

decision_facts.description: The procedure's `handoff.card_fields`, filled — null when unknown.

checks.description: What a person must check, since no tool could.

ai_statements.description: The AI's last messages to the player in the connection (at most 5), oldest first.

output_check_flags.description:
What the draft checks found on the AI's replies. Empty: no
promise was caught.

reason_codes.description: Every reason the AI handed over for, most severe first.

requested_via.description:
`button`: the player pressed "Talk to an agent". Null: the
AI's own decision, or what the player wrote.

suggested_next_step.description: The procedure's `handoff.next_step_hint`, filled; null without one.

card_text.description:
The card as plain text. The agents-only line in the transcript is
this text without the player's username and email — one event every
viewer reads — and here both are blanked out (`•••`) for a caller
whose role may not see a player's contact details
(`customers.contact.view`).

accepted_by.description: The agent whose first message after the hand-over took it up.

ArchiveConversation.description:
One archive row: one connection. `thread_id` is the row's id
(panel "Chat ID"), `chat_id` the day it belongs to (panel "Thread ID").

username.description:
Typed by the player, unverified. Null when not given or the
caller may not see it (`customers.contact.view`).

assignee.description: Who had the connection — at the close, for a closed one.

group_ids.description:
The team the connection went to; for one opened before that was
recorded, the day's teams.

rating.description: The player's newest rating of this connection.

handled_by.description:
Who answered it, written as it closed. `ai` is ADR-09a's AI
resolution (the one the invoice counts); `human` a person and no
bot; `mixed` the rest. Null while open and for a connection closed
before this was recorded.

risk_flags.description: The kinds of risk flag raised in this connection, cleared ones included.

first_customer_message.description: The player's first message, shortened, sensitive values masked.

ArchiveConversationDetail.description:
One connection in the archive: its row, with the rating in
full and the connection's summary.

Brand.description:
One brand of a license (Multibrand, PRD §5.3). A license may run several
brands under a single subscription; each has its own channels, websites
and widget/security/inbox settings, selected via the `X-SiyahTus-Brand`
header on those resources. Every license has exactly one default brand —
the `Default` it is created with — which cannot be deleted.

name.description: Display name, as shown in the brand switcher.

slug.description: URL-safe identifier, unique within the license.

logo_url.description: Brand logo reference, or null when none is set.

is_default.description:
The license's default brand — the one a request with no
`X-SiyahTus-Brand` header resolves to. Exactly one per license; it
cannot be deleted.

Website.description:
A site a workspace has connected the widget to. Distinct
from a trusted domain: a website is the customer-facing
install record — where the snippet was pasted — while a trusted domain is
the security allowlist that decides whether the widget may mint a token
there. Adding a website does not authorise its origin; the domain must
also be a trusted domain for the widget to work.

brand_id.description: The brand this site belongs to (Multibrand, PRD §5.3).

domain.description: Hostname only — lowercased, no scheme, port or path.

setup.description:
`platform` for a hosted integration (Shopify/WordPress/GTM),
`manual` for a pasted snippet. Per PRD §8.4; the specific platform
icon the UI shows is a presentation mapping, not stored here.

status.description:
`connected` once the widget has completed its first handshake from
this domain; `pending` until then. `error` is reserved for a failed
verification signal, written by the widgets screen.

connected_at.description: When the first handshake was seen, or null while pending.

snippet.description:
The code to paste before `</body>`. Sets `window.__siyahtus` and loads
the async widget loader. Identical across a workspace's sites — the
embedding origin is resolved at runtime — so "get code" per row shows
this same value. It ends with a `<noscript>` link to the hosted Chat
page (`/chat.html?organization_id=…`, WG-15) whose text follows the
workspace's widget language from a fixed list; a snippet pasted
before that line existed is not changed.

ChannelType.description:
A connected omnichannel adapter. SMS is `twilio`, its
provider. `instagram` is DM-only. `telegram` is a bot. The Website widget and e-mail forwarding are not
adapters and are not listed here.

WebhookAction.description:
The workspace event that triggers a delivery. A closed vocabulary so a
typo is rejected at registration rather than silently never firing.

`chat_started` announces a new chat together with its first connection
(`thread_id`); `thread_started` announces a further connection opening
under a chat that already exists — the member back the same day
(`reason: same_day_return`, ID-02). One opening is announced by one of
the two, never both. `chat_deactivated` names the connection that
closed (`thread_id`).

`risk_flag_raised` / `risk_flag_cleared` carry what the flag
is, the chat and the member key — never a word anyone wrote.

AU-03: `chat_rated` is a new vote or a changed one (a comment added to
a vote is not a second judgement), its comment masked.
`ticket_updated` names the fields a person changed (`changed`), the
ticket rules' own changes counted in; `ticket_status_changed` carries
`from` and `to`; `ticket_assigned` the new and the previous assignee
and team; `ticket_message_added` a reply, an internal note or the
player's message, by id, kind and author type — no text. Every one is
sent after its transaction committed, once per change.

Webhook.description:
A registered outbound webhook. The signing secret is
deliberately absent — it is returned only once, by the register call
(see `WebhookRegistration`).

Delivery payloads keep the code names: `chat_id` is the panel's
"Thread ID (günlük)", `thread_id` the panel's "Chat ID (bağlantı)".

url.description: The public http(s) endpoint deliveries are POSTed to.

type.description: Workspace-wide (`license`) or scoped to one bot client (`bot`).

enabled.description: Whether deliveries currently fire for this webhook.

app_id.description:
The automation card this subscription belongs to —
`zapier` or `make` — or null for a hand-registered webhook. A
subscription with an `app_id` exists only while that card is
connected: registering one requires the connection, and
disconnecting the card removes it.

WebhookRegistration.description:
The register response. Carries the signing `secret` in addition to the
webhook fields — the **only** time it is ever returned.

secret.description:
The HMAC signing key. Store it now; it is never shown again.
Deliveries are signed
`HMAC-SHA256(secret, "{timestamp}.{nonce}.{body}")`.

WebhookDelivery.description:
One delivery attempt of a webhook. `event_id` groups the
attempts of one event; `attempt` counts them from 1.

status_code.description: The HTTP status the receiver answered with, if it answered.

error.description:
A short cleaned reason (`http_503`, `ssrf_blocked`, `ECONNREFUSED`):
no secret, token, URL or response body, at most 500 characters.

next_attempt_at.description: When the next automatic try is due (`pending` rows only).

can_redeliver.description: Whether `redeliver` would work on this row.

UploadGrant.description:
Permission to store one file, issued by `POST /uploads` once the
licence's file-sharing rules have accepted the declared type and size
— or, for `purpose: knowledge_document`, once the document rules have.

upload_url.description:
Signed, single-use, and bound to the declared type and length. Send
the bytes here with `PUT` before `expires_at`.

upload_id.description:
The key the file is stored under. What `POST
/knowledge-sources/document` takes for a `knowledge_document`.

file_url.description:
Where the file will be readable, and the value that belongs on an
event's `attachment_url`. Does not expire — it is authorised by
session, and by the licence embedded in the key. Absent for a
`knowledge_document`, which `GET /uploads/{key}` never serves.

name.description: Null for a visitor who never introduced themselves.

email.description: Null when the caller's role may not see a player's contact details (`customers.contact.view`).

username.description: The username the visitor typed into the pre-chat form, unverified. Null when the caller's role may not see a player's contact details (`customers.contact.view`).

chats_count.description:
The customer's conversation days in this workspace — chats, "Thread
ID" in the panel. A chat opened before the daily model spans
several visits and counts once. Counted from conversations, not
read from a stored total.

connections_count.description:
The connections those days held — threads, "Chat ID" in the panel:
one per visit, so a member who came back twice in one day counts one
day and two connections. Reports, SLA, AI resolutions and ratings
are all counted per connection, so this is the figure they agree
with.

table_custom_fields.description:
The contact custom fields flagged `show_in_table`,
with this customer's values — one entry per flagged definition, in
authoring order, `value` null when unset. Empty when the workspace
has flagged none. A subset of the full set `GET /customers/{id}`
returns as `custom_fields`; this is only what the Contacts table
renders as a column.

TicketSla.description:
The ticket's first-response clock. Only an agent's
reply stops it — an internal note or a system line does not. Opened
from a chat, a ticket is outside it (the first reply happened in the
conversation, where it is measured).

first_response_at.description: When an agent first replied; null until then.

first_response_due_at.description:
From this moment a first reply is late. Null when the clock is not
running: answered, solved or closed, merged, opened from a chat, or
no target for the ticket's priority. With business hours on, only
open minutes count toward it.

first_response_breached.description:
The miss was recorded, or the running clock is past its due moment.
Once recorded it stays — a later target change does not undo it.

CustomFieldOption.description:
One choice of a `select` / `multiselect` / `topic` field.
`value` is stored and stays put when the label is reworded; a
multiselect answer is a JSON array of values.

target_group_id.description:
A topic's routing: the team a conversation opened with this choice
goes to. Only on a `topic` field. A team deleted since is ignored
and the routing rules decide.

CustomFieldValue.description:
A custom field as it appears on one entity: the
definition's metadata joined with the stored value, or null when nothing
is set. One entry per definition, so a defined-but-empty field still
shows.

options.description: The definition's choices, so a stored value can be shown by its label.

value.description: The stored value in canonical form, or null when unset.

form_placement.description:
Carried through from the definition: lets a reader —
the Traffic visitor 360° panel — tell a form answer apart from a
plain CRM field without a second lookup. On a `ticket` field this is
either `ticket`, a question the visitor answered when they left the
message, or null for a field only an agent fills in.

show_in_table.description:
Carried through from the definition: whether this
field also renders as a row-inline column on the Contacts table.
Always false on a `ticket` field.

CustomFieldValuesInput.description:
A map of custom field definition id → value, where null clears a field.
Each value is validated against its definition (type + required); a
wrong type or a blank on a required field is a 400.

AgentRole.description:
A member's role in the workspace, highest first (`@siyahtus/types`
`AGENT_ROLES`, RL-01): `owner` (Kurucu, exactly one), `admin`
(Yönetici), `team_lead` (Ekip Lideri), `agent` (Ekip Üyesi).
`viceowner` is the old vice owner, which no new assignment offers:
